Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to all of the following expected outcomes:

- all relevant stakeholders, including consumers, economic and social economy operators and waste managers, have an improved understanding of the technical, environmental, economic and social challenges and benefits to circularity in the footwear industry;

- economic operators and waste managers are provided with evidence-based, innovative, cost-effective, and scalable solutions that improve the management of end-of-life footwear products, valorise post-consumer footwear waste materials and increase the circularity of the value chain;

- consumers have access to user-friendly solutions to correctly dispose of end-of-life footwear, thus reducing landfill, improving sustainability practices, supporting them in making more conscious choices, and contributing to climate change mitigation and adaptation by reducing waste and promoting circular economy practices.

Scope:

The transition to a circular economy requires innovative solutions to manage end-of-life products, including footwear, which can have significant environmental and climate impacts if landfilled and not properly collected, sorted, and recycled. In line with the EU's ambitious circular economy targets and policies, such as the Waste Framework Directive and the Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation, this topic aims at improving the circularity of the footwear value chain and reducing the environmental footprint of end-of-life post-consumer footwear, whilst promoting a more regenerative and restorative approach to the footwear value chain.

Proposals should:

- assess the technical, environmental, economic and social challenges and benefits linked to the transition of the footwear industry towards circularity, particularly in the collection, sorting and recycling of post-consumer footwear waste;

- develop and test new methods and technologies that facilitate the collection, sorting, preparation for reuse and recycling of post-consumer footwear products, integrating digital tools (including AI) and the use of the Digital Product Passport to enable reuse and recycling, and minimise the release of hazardous chemicals and microplastics during the recycling process;

- explore and develop innovative business models that enable the transition towards a circular and sustainable footwear value chain, promote the uptake of design for preparing for reuse and recycling, enable the development of take-back solutions and stimulate informed consumer choices and sustainable consumption patterns;

- develop and test innovative solutions that facilitate the collaboration between the relevant stakeholders, including footwear manufacturers, retailers, consumers and waste managers, to ensure the effectiveness and uptake of the proposed solutions, including strategies for managing hazardous chemicals and microplastics in footwear waste.

Successful proposals should bring together all relevant stakeholders active in the footwear value chain, namely industry representatives, SMEs, brand owners, producers, retailers, local authorities, waste managers, economic operators, consumer organisations, researchers, and NGOs.

The topic supports EU policies, particularly the European Green Deal, the Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation and its working plan, as well as the zero pollution action plan. The proposed solutions should also be consistent with the Waste Framework Directive, the Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) for textiles, the Clean Industrial Deal and the EU Circular Economy Act, supporting Europe’s efforts to develop a single market for sustainable products.

This topic requires the effective contribution of SSH disciplines and the involvement of SSH experts, institutions as well as the inclusion of relevant SSH expertise, in order to produce meaningful and significant effects enhancing the societal impact of the related research activities.

Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

- Increased economically viable and functionally equivalent renewable material and sustainable chemical solutions used in large scale textile applications, including apparel, home and technical textiles;

- A realistic pathway for an absolute reduction of the use of virgin fossil-based materials and chemicals used to produce textile products for the EU market by 2035, contributing to enhance the preservation of human health, biodiversity and ecosystems, whether aquatic or terrestrial ecosystem preservation and emission reduction;

- Uptake of business models and system approaches that allow for the scale up of sustainable textile material and chemical alternatives as competitive alternatives to conventional approaches.

Scope:

Innovative renewable textile fibres and sustainable chemical solutions today face almost insurmountable cost disadvantages compared to extremely cost-competitive and industrially entrenched fibres and chemicals based on virgin fossil resources. To allow for the scale up of the use of innovative renewable materials and sustainable chemicals by the textile industry, improved processability of materials, suitable processing technology, deeper technical knowledge and smart phase-in approaches such as material blending or drop-in solutions are required. Specific emphasis must be placed on resulting final product quality, their durability and functionality to avoid negative user/consumer perception of products made with renewable materials and sustainable chemicals. As not all cost and quality challenges may be immediately overcome by technological innovation, accompanying business models and systems approaches are needed to enable equitable cost and risk sharing among all involved stakeholders in the textile value chain.

Attributes such as recyclability, recycled material content, and resource efficiency as well as reduced carbon and environmental footprint are expected to be part of the textile-specific requirements under the Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation.

Proposals should specifically address:

- Innovative processing technologies to facilitate the efficient use of recycled, regenerated and bio-based fibres as well as sustainable processing and functionalising chemicals across all major stages of the textile manufacturing value chain, such as spinning, weaving, knitting, dyeing or finishing;

- Quantification of biodiversity outcomes associated to new processes by using existing Monitoring, Reporting and Validation (MRV) methodologies, adapting and testing them if needed;

- Characterisation, quality assurance and mitigation strategies for the most common processing and functionality challenges and limitations of the sustainable materials and chemicals targeted;

- Development of best practices and training materials targeted at designers, manufacturers, brands, end of life managers and end users, working with the targeted materials and chemicals;

- Strategies and tools to practically implement collective risk sharing and smart scaling approaches.

Proposals should actively involve suppliers of renewable materials and sustainable chemicals, brands, commercial end users and developers/manufacturers of relevant processing technology and industrial partners with the capacity to commercially scale up production with the targeted materials and chemicals. The involvement of partners beyond the manufacturing supply chain, such as product designers, brands, commercial end users and end of life managers including collectors, sorters, recyclers and remanufacturers is particularly encouraged. Proposals should carry out research and innovation to develop missing elements and achieve the necessary integration, including economic viability. The validation and demonstration of new ocean energy technologies should be done in a controlled environment meaning that this is done under monitored and reproducible conditions, using for instance, test rigs and test tanks, semi-enclosed basins, or dedicated real-sea demonstration sites with instrumented monitoring infrastructure.

final_text:
Here's where **Plastic pathways** (#2) stands, what's new on its slate, and one funding lead.

## Where the project stands

- **Focus:** tracing floating debris from river mouths to beaches using forecast currents and satellite detections, to target clean-ups.
- **Current status:** satellite debris detections run weekly; the beaching model is being validated against last summer's beach surveys.
- **Progress:** 35%.
- **Members:** you, Priya Raman, and Jonah Whitcombe.
- **Caveat:** the project's state has never been confirmed by its members, so treat the 35% figure and status line as possibly out of date. If anything has changed, you can update the project in the app.

## Three most relevant new papers

1. **#10 — "A tide-resolving beaching kernel for marine litter"** (Lim & Hong, 2026, Zenodo). The closest match on the slate: a three-phase beaching kernel for OceanParcels, validated against field records from Uido, Korea, using ROMS flow fields. This speaks directly to the open work of checking your beaching model against beach surveys — it's a useful methodological reference and a validation template.
2. **#8 — "Latent-space data assimilation (LSDA)"** (Cornelio et al., 2026). A deep-learning approach to feature-based analysis and forecasting. Relevant to the "forecast currents" half of the project: if you want to move from raw model output toward learned, feature-based state estimates for the particle tracking, this is the paper to read.
3. **#9 — "Daily Analyses of the Pacific Regional Ocean Forecast System model"** (Zhang, 2026, Zenodo). A data release of daily analyses from a regional ocean forecast system. Relevant as a potential source of the current/forecast fields your Lagrangian tracking runs on, and as a template for how to structure and document a recurring analysis product.

(The other new slate items — #3 diatom viromics, #6 chlorophyll-a, #7 algal blooms, #12 fish thermal adaptation — are further afield from debris pathways.)

## One funding opportunity

**#4 — "A stronger Global Ocean Observing System to enhance Europe's strategic autonomy, climate resilience and biodiversity conservation"** (Horizon Europe, HORIZON-NATURE-2027-04-01). €50,000,000, still open, application deadline **16 February 2027**.

- **What fits:** the call funds strengthening global ocean observing — deploying observation equipment, observing-system experiments, network optimization, and technology roadmaps with industry. Your project's satellite debris detection pipeline is exactly the kind of novel observing capability it asks for, and your lab's declared profile (satellite ocean remote sensing, debris pathways, tools for coastal managers) lines up with its emphasis on fit-for-purpose observation and data delivery.
- **The biggest doubt:** the call's scope is global and institutional — it focuses on areas beyond national jurisdiction, GOOS governance, and large-scale network deployment, and at €50M it is almost certainly a consortium-scale call. A single lab's debris-tracking project would need to be framed as a component of a broader observing-system proposal, and I can't see the eligibility rules (EU member-state requirements, consortium size) from here — check those in the call text before committing.

**Suggested next steps:** confirm the project's state in the app so the record is current; read #10's method in full before the next beaching-model validation round; and if the GOOS call interests you, sketch how the satellite debris detection work would slot into a consortium proposal well before the February deadline.

final_text:
Here's what I found, in three parts.

## Best fit: #13 Green, circular and resilient harbours

Of the open grants in the corpus, #13 is the closest to Plastic pathways (#2). The call asks for place-based, people-centred actions that reduce pollution in harbour areas, with strong involvement of port authorities and local communities, and it explicitly encourages monitoring the effectiveness of the solutions. That lines up with the project's core: satellite debris detections, forecast currents, and a beaching model used to target clean-ups (#2). The strongest reason is that the project's detection-and-targeting pipeline is exactly the kind of "systemic innovative solution" the call wants demonstrated and monitored in real ports. The biggest doubt: the call requires demonstration in at least 4 ports across four different sea basins, with public port authorities as partners — that's a much bigger consortium build-out than the project's current river-mouth-to-beach scope, and the project's state has never been confirmed by its members.

The other open calls I checked are further away: #6 (microplastics coordination center) is biomedical and US-based; #9 (waterborne transport) is about zero-carbon fuel spills; #3 (biotech recycling) is industrial material science; #21 (Global Ocean Observing System) is a €50M infrastructure call focused on biodiversity EOVs and areas beyond national jurisdiction; #29 (coastal resilience) is about climate adaptation and nature-based solutions, not pollution tracking.

## Who in the lab should lead

The nightly ranking named **Jonah Whitcombe (#37)** as the closest profile match to this call (64%), ahead of **Priya Raman (#38)** (63%) and you (59%). That makes sense from what's declared:

- **Jonah** declared marine litter and Lagrangian analysis — the heart of the project's debris-tracking method.
- **Priya** declared satellite oceanography and coastal water quality — the detection side.
- **You** are the PI and project owner, so you'd naturally anchor the application even if Jonah leads the scientific core.

One honest caveat: none of the lab's declared profiles covers the call's key requirement slots — port authorities, public administrations, and the 4-port demonstration structure. Those are consortium roles, not researcher roles, so the "lead" question is really about who writes the scientific case (Jonah, with Priya) while you build the port-authority partnerships.

## Who outside the lab

I can't suggest specific people here: collaborator search is turned off on this instance, so I have no consented names to point you to. What the call itself tells you is who you need: **public port managing authorities and local administrations** in at least four ports, one in each of the Atlantic/Arctic, Mediterranean, Baltic/North Sea, and Danube basins (#13). The call strongly encourages these public bodies as consortium partners, so your first outreach should be to port authorities in the basins where your river-mouth-to-beach data already has coverage.

## Timeline

#13 is open with a deadline of **21 September 2027** — about ten months away, which is workable for building a multi-port consortium. If you want, I can pull the project's current slate or check what's already saved for this call.

#16 [grant] Expeditionary Water Quality Sensors
Link: https://www.sbir.gov/topics/13112
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-01-06
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Current water quality testing kits for expeditionary forces are too cumbersome, complex, and slow, often requiring chemical reagents, extensive training, and external laboratory confirmation, which creates logistics burdens or health risks in contested environments.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Development of new sensors and/or methodologies to improve field kits, focusing on reducing size, weight, testing time, and complexity while eliminating liquid chemical reagents.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Expeditionary, austere, and contested environments involving small, distributed Stand-in Forces (squad- and platoon-level).
Abstract:
Expeditionary forces need updated water testing capabilities to support operations in austere, contested environments. Without proper water testing, water purified in the field are not certified potable for consumption. This creates an unacceptable logistics burden to transport water, or a health risks when consuming untested water; hindering the self-sufficiency, readiness, and lethality required for operations against a pacing challenge. Current approved state-of-the-art water quality testing kits are accurate but cumbersome, and overly complex, requiring chemical reagents, significant operator training, and for some parameters shipping to a certified lab. Present water quality testing methods are not practical for the small, distributed Stand-in Forces operating in expeditionary conditions.

In the event of detection of certain pathogens and contaminants, confirmation through certified laboratories may be required, necessitating sample transportation to CONUS, host-nation, or ally facilities—a process that can take 4-6 weeks. Delays of this magnitude are operationally unacceptable for forces in contested environments that need immediate assurance of water safety at the point of use. In addition, many critical parameters that impact water safety—including heavy metals, organic chemicals, and other contaminants—are not reliably tested with currently fielded sensors.

Force Design 2030 compels distributed forces to reduce their reliance on centralized logistics convoys; therefore, small units are increasingly required to produce and consume water at the tactical edge and at the point of need. Without a reliable and practical method to verify water quality in the field, these units face an alarming tradeoff between logistics supply certainty and warfighter health.

Therefore, the Navy needs simple, field-ready solutions to certify that expeditionary purified water conforms to TB-MED 577 short term potability military field water standards (STW MFWS) without external laboratory support. This SBIR topic seeks the development of new sensors and/or methodologies that will significantly improve existing water testing field kits. Improvements sought include but are not limited to: size and weight, more rapid testing results, simpler procedures requiring minimal training, elimination of liquid chemical reagents, and cost. Proposals can address one or more targeted improvements and can target one or more of the water parameters listed in the STP MFWS, such as physical properties, chemical properties, microbial contamination, chemical warfare agents, or radiological. Resulting improved sensors or methodologies must be integratable into future modernized water testing kits to allow squad- and platoon-level forces to verify compliance with TB MED 577 water safety standards in the field, reducing risk to personnel and decreasing reliance on vulnerable resupply chains. The expected end state of this effort is a fully developed, ruggedized, integratable sensor or set of sensors that enable rapid, automated testing of water quality in expeditionary environments in under 15 minutes (Threshold) / under 5 minutes (Objective), and/or detect all microbial threats in under 1 hour (Threshold) / under 15 minutes (Objective) without incubation or liquid reagents. Modular systems targeting specific critical parameters are equally encouraged and will be evaluated on technical merit.

Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

This topic aims at directly engaging with and supporting riparian and coastal areas, waterfront cities and islands and their communities in demonstrating and accelerating the transitions needed for achieving one or several objectives of the Mission “Restore our Ocean and Waters”. The participation of relevant public bodies managing those areas and their communities as partners of the consortium is strongly encouraged.

Project results are expected to contribute to all the following outcomes:

- Member States and Associated Countries are provided with cost-effective and innovative solutions to increasing riparian and coastal areas’ resilience to climate change, especially in waterfront cities and islands, contributing to reach the targets of the EU climate adaptation and water resilience strategies for 2030, but also supporting achievements of the EU biodiversity strategy for 2030, the Water Framework and the Marine Strategy Framework directives;

- Enhanced ecological functions of riparian and coastal areas including in waterfront cities and islands (e.g.: water quality improvement, pollution remediation, erosion control, morpho-dynamics and sediment transport, biodiversity conservation and restoration);

- Reduced vulnerability to climate change related risks (e.g.: lowering flood risks by increasing their natural buffer capacity; adapting to sea level rises and extreme events, and enhancing drought resilience by increasing groundwater recharge functions, carbon sequestration, reducing harmful algal blooms, etc.) with biodiversity co-benefits;

- Increased socio-economic benefits deriving from protecting and restoring riparian and coastal areas and from the remediation of pollution, as well as for recreational and touristic activities;

- Stakeholders and local competent authorities managing riparian and coastal areas, including in waterfront cities and islands (not limited only to those who are partners in the consortium), are engaged to implement and upscale innovative solutions that contribute to increasing resilience to climate change and water-related risks, including by strengthening synergies with their own programmes and resources and encouraging public and private investment.

Scope:

Riparian and coastal areas play a critical role in local climate regulation and serve as the buffer regions between land and waterways, providing a wide array of important ecosystem services such as acting as natural barriers against storm surges, flooding, and erosion, filtering pollutants from the water, regulating floods, providing habitats for species and increasing soil health. sequestering carbon. Islands, which offer invaluable natural resources that support people, cultures and livelihoods, are particularly vulnerable to climate change.[1]

The proposal should build (when relevant) on previously developed or existing solutions by other projects, funded by EU and national programmes, in particular the European Union Framework programmes for Research and Innovation [2], the co-funded Partnership Water Security for the Planet (Water4All)[3] as well as ERDF, INTERREG and LIFE programmes. Proposals are also encouraged to consider -- where relevant -- the services offered by European research infrastructures[4]. final_text:
Here's the picture across both projects, based on what's in each project's current slate.

## The two most urgent deadlines

**1. #6 — 10th International Conference on Geoinformatics and Data Analysis (ICGDA 2027)**
- Manuscript due **2026-11-20 — 4 days away**; event April 2027
- In the slate of **#1 Marine heatwave early warning** (entered 2026-11-10)
- **Who fits:** the nightly ranking named **Priya Raman** as the closest profile match (59%), with you (58%) and **Jonah Whitcombe** (58%) close behind. Priya's declared satellite oceanography plus your data-assimilation-with-ML profile make the two of you the natural lead pair; Jonah could carry a debris-detection angle if you want to bridge projects.
- **Paper that would strengthen it:** **#38 — "Evaluation of 1-14-Day Machine-Learning Forecasts of Marine Heatwaves in the Northern Bay of Bengal Against Persistence Benchmarks"** (Mojumder, 2026). It's the closest published analogue to your project's core claim — ML MHW forecasts evaluated against persistence — and your hindcasts already beat persistence at four weeks, so it's a direct benchmark to cite and, if your results are stronger, to beat.

**2. #46 — 19th International Conference on Computer Modeling and Simulation (ICCMS 2027)**
- Manuscript due **2026-12-10 — 24 days away**; event May 2027
- In the slate of **#1 Marine heatwave early warning** (entered 2026-11-13)
- **Who fits:** Mylo hasn't read this call's requirement slots yet, so it named no one from the lab. Judging from declared profiles, **Tomás Ferreira-Lind** (circulation and turbulence, physics-informed ML) is the best fit for a modeling-and-simulation venue, with **Sun-hee Park** (ocean data tools) as a natural co-author on the dashboard/delivery side.
- **Paper that would strengthen it:** **#29 — "An end-to-end machine-learning system for global eddy-resolving ocean forecast"** (Zhang et al., *Science Advances*, 2026). It's the strongest recent demonstration that an ML system can replace the whole numerical forecast pipeline and outperform a state-of-the-art numerical GOFS — exactly the kind of result a modeling-and-simulation audience wants to see, and it supports your ML-corrected ensemble approach.

## Worth flagging

- Both urgent deadlines sit in the **marine heatwave** project. The **Plastic pathways** project's nearest deadline is **#24 — 47th IEEE IGARSS**, abstract and manuscript due **2027-01-11** (about 7 weeks out). If you want a plastic-pathways submission in the same window, that's the one to start on; **#30** (the tide-resolving beaching kernel for marine litter, Lim & Hong, 2026) would be the paper to anchor it, since your beaching model is currently being checked against last summer's beach surveys.
- The two biggest grants in either slate — **#23** (EU GOOS, €50M, due 2027-02-16) and **#33** (NSF OTIC, due 2027-02-15) — are both in February, so they're not urgent yet, but they're the ones worth planning around next.

One caveat: the deadline list I pulled covers the next 60 days (20 of 64 shown), so anything between mid-January and mid-February isn't in that window — the February grants above come from the project slates, not the deadline list.

#36 [paper] Marine heatwave forecast triggers rapid response strategy for critically endangered red handfish
Authors: Jemina Stuart‐Smith, Tyson J. Bessell, Alistair James Hobday, Rick D. Stuart‐Smith, Ness Delpero, Victor Shelamoff, SD Ling, Tara Kelly
Venue: Conservation Science and Practice
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1111/csp2.70439
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Preventing extinction of the Critically Endangered red handfish (Thymichthys politus) during acute marine heatwaves (MHW) driven by climate change.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A proactive, pre-emptive rescue strategy triggered by climate forecasts and expert workshop assessment, involving the temporary capture of wild individuals, holding them in captivity for three months, and releasing them after the heatwave subsided.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Wild population of red handfish in Australia during the 2023/2024 El Niño event, specifically January 2024, with in situ water temperatures exceeding records.
Abstract:
Abstract As climate change drives increasingly frequent and severe climatic extremes, effective strategies to prevent extinction of threatened species are urgently needed. Interventions enabling species to survive acute stress may buy time to address other threats and identify long‐term refugia. For the Critically Endangered red handfish ( Thymichthys politus ), forecasts ahead of the 2023/2024 El Niño indicated a high risk of marine heatwaves (MHW). An expert workshop identified these forecasted extremes (>20 or +~3°C) as a severe threat, triggering an emergency rescue to temporarily remove individuals from the wild. Following commonwealth, state and institutional approvals, 25 fish were captured in January 2024 and held in captivity for 3 months. During this period, in situ water temperatures exceeded records, including 80 days more than 2°C above the long‐term mean summer temperature (~17.5°C). Three fish died in captivity and four adults were retained in a captive breeding program, while the remaining 18 individuals were returned after the MHW subsided, with post‐release survival confirmed after 2 months. This represents Australia's first pre‐emptive rescue of a protected marine species and highlights the importance of proactive, adaptive conservation to strengthen capacity in safeguarding threatened species during environmental extremes and long term climate change impacts.

#40 [paper] A Deep Learning Framework for Automatic Detection and Segmentation of Internal Solitary Waves in Satellite Imagery over the Northern South China Sea
Authors: Guocai Rong, Huanhe Dong, Yuan Kong, Ze Liu, Yong Hui Fang
Venue: Remote Sensing
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3390/rs18213843
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Automated extraction of internal solitary waves (ISWs) from satellite imagery is challenging due to their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast.
Method (Mycelium's reading): YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint detection and pixel-level segmentation, incorporating Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) for curved structures and the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) for low-contrast features.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea; the framework was also applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020.
Abstract:
Internal solitary waves (ISWs) play an important role in ocean energy transport and mixing, yet their elongated, curved crest lines and low contrast make automated extraction from satellite imagery challenging. To address these challenges, this study proposes YOLO11-ISW, an improved YOLO11-based framework for joint ISW detection and pixel-level segmentation. Dynamic Snake Convolution (DSConv) is introduced to enhance the representation of curved crest-line structures, while the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) strengthens responses to low-contrast ISW features. A MODIS-based ISW dataset from the northern South China Sea was constructed for model training and evaluation. YOLO11-ISW achieved detection Precision, Recall, and F1-score values of 92.01%, 80.73%, and 86.00%, respectively, and segmentation values of 93.14%, 82.60%, and 87.55%, respectively. The model achieved the highest detection and segmentation F1-scores among the evaluated methods. The segmentation results were further georeferenced to extract ISW crest-line locations, and the framework was applied to MODIS imagery from 2011 to 2020 to investigate satellite-observed ISW spatiotemporal variability. The detected ISWs exhibited pronounced spatial clustering, strong spring–summer seasonality, and clear lunar-cycle modulation, consistent with previous observations in the northern South China Sea. These results demonstrate the potential of YOLO11-ISW for automated, long-term, and large-scale monitoring of ISWs using satellite remote sensing imagery.

Abstract:
Machine learning (ML) models, especially those based on deep neural networks, have achieved competitive forecast accuracy and greatly reduced computational burden compared to traditional numerical global ocean forecast systems (GOFSs). However, it remains difficult for these ML models to operate on their own, as they rely on the initial conditions generated by numerical GOFSs. In this study, we present WenHai-E2E, an end-to-end ML GOFS that replaces the entire pipeline of numerical GOFSs at deployment time and makes eddy-resolving global ocean forecast directly from multisource heterogeneous ocean observations, without requiring operational initial conditions from numerical GOFSs. Our results demonstrate the promise of ML GOFSs to surpass numerical GOFSs and provide insight into the pathway for developing next generation of GOFSs.

#35 [paper] Vertical structure and evolution of large-scale subsurface marine heatwaves
Authors: Shujing Zhang, Neil J. Holbrook, Alex Sen Gupta, Annie Foppert, Zijie Zhao
Venue: npj Climate and Atmospheric Science
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41612-026-01592-5
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The vertical structure and evolution of large-scale subsurface marine heatwaves (MHWs) are poorly understood due to sparse long-record subsurface observations and a lack of globally consistent characterization frameworks.
Method (Mycelium's reading): A four-dimensional event-tracking framework applied to ocean temperature reanalysis data, utilizing depth rescaling and cluster analysis to identify vertical structure types.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Ocean temperature reanalysis data for the upper 1000 m of the near-global ocean (60°N–60°S) from 1993–2020.
Abstract:
Abstract Subsurface marine heatwaves (MHWs) represent hidden thermal extremes that can strongly impact marine ecosystems, particularly when they are large-scale and long-lasting. Although they evolve across time and space, their vertical structure and evolution remain poorly understood because of sparse long-record subsurface observations and the limited application of globally consistent frameworks to characterize them. Here we apply a four-dimensional event-tracking framework to ocean temperature reanalysis data to identify and characterize over 500 large-scale subsurface MHWs in the upper 1000 m of the near-global ocean (60°N–60°S) from 1993–2020. Occurrences are highest in equatorial regions and lowest in the subtropics. The framework captures extensive subsurface expressions of major events, including the northeast Pacific Blob, which penetrated hundreds of metres below the surface, and the Ningaloo Niño, whose subsurface structure extended beyond its traditionally defined surface footprint. Using depth rescaling and cluster analysis, we identify seven recurring vertical structure types, with five significantly associated with El Niño–Southern Oscillation phases. MHWs generally maintain their vertical structure for months to years, with limited propagation across the mixed layer and thermocline. Together, these findings link subsurface MHW evolution to large-scale climate variability and ocean stratification, providing a basis for improved detection and potential predictability.

#59 [paper] Gap filling of missing and invalid values in SWOT wide-swath sea surface height data using Attention U-Net
Authors: 时高琛, Jungang Yang, Yongjun Jia, Wei Cui
Venue: Remote Sensing Letters
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1080/2150704x.2026.2760394
Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Spatial discontinuities in SWOT Level-3 wide-swath sea surface height (SSH) data caused by the 20-km nadir gap and invalid data regions.
Method (Mycelium's reading): An Attention U-Net-based gap-filling model trained on simulated SWOT SSH data generated from GLORYS12V1 reanalysis data.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Global SWOT wide-swath observations, validated against SWOT nadir and Sentinel-6A altimeter data, with specific focus on the Kuroshio Extension and Gulf Stream regions.
Abstract:
High-resolution sea surface height (SSH) data are essential for studying mesoscale and submesoscale ocean dynamics. The Surface Water and Ocean Topography (SWOT) satellite, launched on 16 December 2022, provides high-resolution SSH observations over a 120-km swath. However, the 20-km nadir gap and invalid data regions in SWOT Level-3 products create spatial discontinuities, limiting continuous observations of fine-scale ocean processes. To address this problem, an Attention U-Net-based gap-filling model is proposed to fill both the nadir gap and invalid data regions in SWOT wide-swath SSH data. Simulated SWOT SSH data were generated from GLORYS12V1 reanalysis data along SWOT Level-3 ground tracks and used to train the model. The trained model was then applied to global SWOT wide-swath observations. Results show that the proposed method outperforms inverse distance weighting, cubic spline interpolation, optimal interpolation and U-Net. Validation against SWOT nadir and Sentinel-6A altimeter data shows strong agreement, with RMSE of 2.3–3.2 cm, R2 of 0.889–0.945, and bias of 0.28 cm. Submesoscale spatial features and spectral consistency are well preserved in energetic regions, including the Kuroshio Extension and Gulf Stream, supporting SWOT applications.

Here's what I can tell you, in three parts.

## Best-fit open grant: #3 (Integrating Remote Sensing and in-situ observations of Biodiversity)

Of the open grants in the project's slate, #3 is the closest match to Plastic pathways (#1). The call asks for multisensory data-integration systems that harmonize in-situ observations with satellite remote sensing and AI analytics, with demonstration cases in marine ecosystems under pressure — and the project already runs weekly satellite debris detections and is validating a beaching model against in-situ beach surveys. That's the same integration problem the call is funding, just aimed at debris rather than species.

The biggest doubt: the call is biodiversity-framed (habitat mapping, ecosystem condition, EU typology), so the proposal would need to argue that debris tracking is a pressure on those ecosystems — which is defensible, but it's a stretch from the project's core. The deadline is 2027-09-22, so there's time.

Runners-up, and why they're weaker:
- **#9 (Global Ocean Observing System, €50M, deadline 2027-02-16)** — strong on the satellite/observing-systems side, but it's a €50M infrastructure-scale call focused on GOOS governance, areas beyond national jurisdiction, and biodiversity EOVs. Plastic pathways is a small project; this is a consortium-scale call.
- **#18 (NSF OTIC, deadline 2027-02-15)** — only fits if you frame it as developing new debris-detection instrumentation; the project is currently detection-and-modeling, not instrument development.
- **#4 (Green, circular and resilient harbours, deadline 2027-09-21)** — pollution-reduction in ports, but it requires demonstration in at least 4 ports across four basins with port authorities as partners. That's a different shape of project.

## Who should lead

**Jonah Whitcombe (#14)** is the natural lead: he's a project member and his declared interests are marine litter and Lagrangian analysis — the exact core of the project.

**Priya Raman (#15)** is the strongest technical contributor: her declared satellite ocean remote sensing covers the call's "satellite-based Earth observation data" slot — the only slot anyone in the lab covers. The nightly ranking also named her and you for #3.

**You** should be the PI/co-lead: the ranking named you for #3, and as PI you carry the data-assimilation and ML angle the call's AI-analytics requirement needs.

Gaps no one in the lab covers: omics-based data, in-situ biodiversity data frameworks (GBIF/OBIS-type), and Copernicus/Galileo. You'd need partners for those.

## Partners outside the lab

I have to be straight with you: **collaborator search is turned off on this instance**, so I can't name specific people outside the lab. What I can say from the call's requirements is what the consortium needs:

- A **biodiversity/ecosystem-assessment group** to carry the in-situ biodiversity data and EU ecosystem typology framing (the call's core, and the lab's biggest gap)
- An **omics or in-situ data-frameworks group** (GBIF/OBIS-type infrastructure)
- A **Copernicus/Earth-observation data partner** for the satellite side

results.name: read_skill
results.content:
# Judging a call's fit

1. Read the call with `corpus_item` (deadlines, eligibility, amount, whether it is
   still open). If it is closed, say so first.
2. Read who it is for: `projects_get` for a project, `org_lab` for a lab,
   `me_profile` / `me_interests` for the person.
3. Compare concretely: the call's aims against the project's problem and
   method; its eligibility rules (career stage, citizenship, institution type)
   against what you know; its deadline against the project's milestones.
4. Say what fits, what does not, and what you could not check (eligibility you
   cannot see, a budget you do not know). Never guess eligibility.
5. If the question is who should apply, read the `who-should-apply` skill.

Honesty rules, as in Mylo's reports: no scores or percentages, no hype, no
"perfect fit". One plain sentence on the strongest reason and one on the
biggest doubt. Cite the call and the project by #n.

# Who should apply

1. Read the call (`corpus_item`). Then `knowledge_people_for_call`, which
   returns, per person, the requirement slots they cover and the evidence tier
   of each: **declared** (they said so in their profile), **demonstrated**
   (their own papers), **confirmed in conversation** (they told Mylo and said
   yes when asked).
2. Present people by the slots they cover, strongest evidence first. Say the
   tier in plain words for each claim ("from her papers", "she told Mylo in
   October").
3. Name gaps: slots no one covers. Outside-the-lab suggestions only appear when
   collaborator search is on and people consented; never speculate beyond them.
4. Do not rank people with numbers, and do not judge anyone's eligibility you
   cannot see.

Problem (Mycelium's reading): Existing in-situ biodiversity data collections (genomic, ground, drone) lack the structure, interface, and metadata required for integration with satellite remote sensing and advanced AI analytics, hindering the assessment of ecosystem condition and biodiversity trends.

Setting (Mycelium's reading): Terrestrial, freshwater, and marine ecosystems in EU Member States and Associated Countries, specifically focusing on ecosystems under pressure or restoration priorities within the EU ecosystem typology.
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to all of the following expected outcomes:

- advancing robust, policy-relevant ecosystem assessment, nature protection and restoration planning activities, and biodiversity trend prediction based on fit for purpose data, thus supporting EU biodiversity and climate objectives;

- strengthened capacity of researchers, practitioners and decision-makers to improve biodiversity monitoring practices and address knowledge gaps via the integration of data and observations across sensors and platforms, ranging from omics-based data (genomic, transcriptomic, metabolomic), various in-situ to satellite-based Earth observation data;

- enhanced usability of in-situ datasets as training and validation resources for statistical, machine learning and advanced AI-based approaches, in support of applications such as habitat classification, ecosystem mapping and biodiversity trend prediction.

Scope:

Achieving the goals of the EU biodiversity strategy for 2030, the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, and assessing progress towards their defined targets, requires coherent, integrated and long-term monitoring approaches, underpinned by FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable and Re-usable) data systems. Many existing in-situ data collections (i.e. genomic assessments, ground sampling, drone and airborne observations) were not designed with Satellite Remote Sensing integration in mind (i.e. for validation and calibration, integrated data products, or statistical scaling of information) and lack the structure, interface and metadata required to support advanced analytics, including AI. FAIR data on species and ecosystems will also help to ensure that biodiversity preservation is a mainstream feature of other sectors, such as agriculture, transport, energy or the bioeconomy. There is a need for systemic, harmonised or standardised biodiversity data at Earth’s surface in order to support AI applications ranging from genome to space and to build up our knowledge on the status and trends of habitats, species, ecosystems, and on the drivers of decline.

- develop concrete technical capabilities able to answer to diverse use cases, across terrestrial, freshwater and marine ecosystems in Member States and Associated Countries. #5 [grant] Expeditionary Water Quality Sensors
Link: https://www.sbir.gov/topics/13112
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-01-06
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Current water quality testing kits for expeditionary forces are too cumbersome, complex, and slow, often requiring chemical reagents, extensive training, and external laboratory confirmation, which creates logistics burdens or health risks in contested environments.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Development of new sensors and/or methodologies to improve field kits, focusing on reducing size, weight, testing time, and complexity while eliminating liquid chemical reagents.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Expeditionary, austere, and contested environments involving small, distributed Stand-in Forces (squad- and platoon-level).
Abstract:
Expeditionary forces need updated water testing capabilities to support operations in austere, contested environments. Without proper water testing, water purified in the field are not certified potable for consumption. This creates an unacceptable logistics burden to transport water, or a health risks when consuming untested water; hindering the self-sufficiency, readiness, and lethality required for operations against a pacing challenge. Current approved state-of-the-art water quality testing kits are accurate but cumbersome, and overly complex, requiring chemical reagents, significant operator training, and for some parameters shipping to a certified lab. Present water quality testing methods are not practical for the small, distributed Stand-in Forces operating in expeditionary conditions.

In the event of detection of certain pathogens and contaminants, confirmation through certified laboratories may be required, necessitating sample transportation to CONUS, host-nation, or ally facilities—a process that can take 4-6 weeks. Delays of this magnitude are operationally unacceptable for forces in contested environments that need immediate assurance of water safety at the point of use. In addition, many critical parameters that impact water safety—including heavy metals, organic chemicals, and other contaminants—are not reliably tested with currently fielded sensors.

Force Design 2030 compels distributed forces to reduce their reliance on centralized logistics convoys; therefore, small units are increasingly required to produce and consume water at the tactical edge and at the point of need. Without a reliable and practical method to verify water quality in the field, these units face an alarming tradeoff between logistics supply certainty and warfighter health.

Therefore, the Navy needs simple, field-ready solutions to certify that expeditionary purified water conforms to TB-MED 577 short term potability military field water standards (STW MFWS) without external laboratory support. This SBIR topic seeks the development of new sensors and/or methodologies that will significantly improve existing water testing field kits. Improvements sought include but are not limited to: size and weight, more rapid testing results, simpler procedures requiring minimal training, elimination of liquid chemical reagents, and cost. Proposals can address one or more targeted improvements and can target one or more of the water parameters listed in the STP MFWS, such as physical properties, chemical properties, microbial contamination, chemical warfare agents, or radiological. Resulting improved sensors or methodologies must be integratable into future modernized water testing kits to allow squad- and platoon-level forces to verify compliance with TB MED 577 water safety standards in the field, reducing risk to personnel and decreasing reliance on vulnerable resupply chains. The expected end state of this effort is a fully developed, ruggedized, integratable sensor or set of sensors that enable rapid, automated testing of water quality in expeditionary environments in under 15 minutes (Threshold) / under 5 minutes (Objective), and/or detect all microbial threats in under 1 hour (Threshold) / under 15 minutes (Objective) without incubation or liquid reagents. Modular systems targeting specific critical parameters are equally encouraged and will be evaluated on technical merit.

results.content:
#10 [grant] Compact Unmanned Aerial System for Marine Species Monitoring
Link: https://www.sbir.gov/topics/13133
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-01-06
Problem (Mycelium's reading): Existing UAS for marine species monitoring are often prohibitively expensive, lack integrated high-resolution photogrammetry capabilities, or fail to meet specific operational requirements (size, duration, and NDAA compliance) for field-based research.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Development of a prototype compact, inexpensive, and NDAA-compliant UAS integrating a high-resolution flat zoom lens camera with a gimbal, a LiDAR altimeter/range finder (50m+), and a lightweight battery system (<100 Wh).
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Small boat-based operations in wet conditions (IP45 rating) with temperatures ranging from -20 to +40 degrees Celsius.
Abstract:
A major remaining hurdle with marine species management is to know if, and when, measurable short-term behavioral and/or physiological responses of marine species to sound exposure results in biologically significant or meaningful effects on individuals and/or their populations. Advances in UAS methods and technology present unprecedented opportunities to improve the capacity to collect this robust data with minimal disturbance to marine species. However, while UAS methods have led to significant advances in our understanding of marine species’ behavior, health, and body condition, thus far many obstacles remain including cost, flight duration, size, and image resolution.

This STTR topic seeks to develop a compact, inexpensive, and NDAA-compliant UAS and payloads designed to collect high-resolution photogrammetry imagery to improve marine mammal monitoring, health measurements, and behavioral sequencing. In particular, the prototype device should contain the following technical parameters: high resolution flat zoom lens camera integrated with a gimbal system; highly maneuverable and flexible payload system; lightweight batteries less than 100 Watt hours; an accurate Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR) altimeter and range finder integrated with the camera and capable of measuring distances up to 50m or more; and a monitor that is operational in direct sunlight and with polarized sunglasses;. It should be designed for flight times as much as or greater than 40 minutes; be compact and portable in both size and weight such that the UAS and case can fit airline luggage restrictions; have the ability to be quickly calibrated, launched, and caught by hand during small boat-based operations and to tolerate temperature range of -20 degrees to +40 degrees Celsius; and have a minimum weather resistant rating of IP45 to allow for operations in wet conditions; be capable of dynamic home point positioning; and produces minimal noise.

While there are several existing NDAA-compliant drones available in the marketplace, the desired components and capabilities only exist in piecemeal and further, these UAS are prohibitively expensive for the field. The DON seeks to develop a prototype device to be designed and optimized for marine species monitoring, encompassing all the above technical parameters. Critically, this device must be affordable for the marine research community with the target market price between $10,000 - $15,000.

Abstract:

Project results are expected to contribute to some of the following expected outcomes:

Understanding the mechanisms and drivers of land (including inland waters) and ocean carbon sinks and sources is crucial for accurate climate models and scenarios and informing climate mitigation strategies. However, significant gaps and uncertainties remain in quantifying these complex processes and their components. It is essential to better understand the roles of anthropogenic and natural drivers of carbon fluxes, in particular the surface-to-air flux. This is necessary for reconciling conceptual discrepancies among estimates and assessing the implications for future trends and mitigation potential, taking into account that mitigation actions need to be additional to natural processes and business-as-usual and that the remaining carbon budget depends, inter alia, on assumptions on sinks.

International cooperation is generally encouraged, in particular with low and lower/upper-middle-income countries[1].

#26 [grant] Innovative Solutions for mitigating the environmental impact of waterborne transport in marine and aquatic Ecosystems (ZEWT Partnership)
Amount: €2,000,000–€13,500,000
Link: https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/portal/screen/opportunities/topic-details/HORIZON-CL5-2027-03-D5-17
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-04-14
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The decarbonization of waterborne transport using renewable low and zero-carbon fuels introduces new, unexplored risks to marine and aquatic ecosystems, including pollution from normal operations and accidental spills, threatening the achievement of Good Environmental and Ecological Status in Europ…
Method (Mycelium's reading): The project aims to evaluate and forecast environmental impacts, model pollution sources, and develop, demonstrate, and test innovative prevention, abatement, and mitigation systems and strategies (targeting TRL 5) for managing spills and reducing harmful impacts of zero-emission fuels.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): European marine waters, inland waterways, and port areas, focusing on waterborne transport operations using renewable low and zero-carbon fuels.
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to all of the following expected outcomes.

- Improved water resilience and good environmental and good ecological status in European waters and contribute to the achievement of the European Union's environmental targets, including the European Water Resilience Strategy and the European Ocean Pact.

- A comprehensive understanding of the future environmental impacts of waterborne transport on marine and other aquatic ecosystems, addressing in particular pollution sources from: i) navigation on renewable low and zero-carbon fuels; and ii) accidental spills of renewable low and zero-carbon fuels for marine waters, inland waters and ports (water and air quality).

- Innovative prevention, abatement and mitigation systems and strategies for reducing and eliminating the harmful impacts of waterborne transport on waters.

- Enhanced pollution prevention and mitigation in marine waters, inland waterways and port areas, reducing the likelihood and impact of accidents involving renewable low and zero-carbon fuels.

Scope:

The European Union aims to protect and conserve its marine and freshwater environments by achieving Good Environmental and Good Ecological Status[1]. The European Water Resilience Strategy and the European Ocean Pact further emphasize the need to enhance the resilience of European waters to human-induced pressures. Projects like the Horizon Europe EMERGE have researched the impacts of shipping on marine ecosystems. The introduction of technologies to decarbonize the sector may enable, to a certain extent, to phase-out relevant current sources of water and air pollution. However, renewable low and zero-carbon fuels and procedures pose new risks to marine and other aquatic ecosystems like rivers and lakes yet to be explored and addressed, both from the normal function of waterborne transport[2] and from accidental spills of renewable low and zero-carbon fuels. In addition, other pollution sources can be addressed today[3]. This topic aims to evaluate, forecast, control and mitigate the impact of waterborne transport on marine and other aquatic ecosystems, with a focus on developing and demonstrating innovative abatement and mitigation systems and strategies to mitigate and eliminate, where possible, the harmful impact of waterborne transport in the ocean and inland waters. New technologies and solutions addressing the decarbonization of waterborne transport will be considered, as well as the potential risks and challenges associated with these.

Actions should address all of the following aspects:

- Evaluate and forecast the environmental impacts of waterborne transport operations on marine, rivers and other aquatic ecosystems, in particular regarding the effects of renewable low and zero-carbon fuels (with particular attention to accidental spills) and related technologies. The proposal may include testing and experimental work in relation with spills.

- Develop and demonstrate effective response scenarios, including the associated abatement technologies and any potential new innovative equipment, for managing uncontrolled releases of renewable low and zero-carbon fuels in marine and inland waters or in port areas, including dedicated specific procedures and operational guidelines.

- Modelling scenarios on water and air pollution sources from each ship types and services running on renewable low and zero carbon fuels.

- Develop and demonstrate innovative and cost-effective abatement and mitigation systems and strategies to prevent, eliminate and reduce the harmful impacts of the use of renewable low and zero carbon fuels. Relevant TRL5 demonstration of such systems should be done.

- Identifying training needs and skills requirements to deploy developed solutions, as well as in relation to the management and use of renewable low carbon fuels in ports and on vessels in marine and inland waters, including relevant emergency response preparedness.

Amount: €1,000,000–€8,925,000
Link: https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/portal/screen/opportunities/topic-details/HORIZON-MISS-2027-03-OCEAN-01
Still open/current: yes

Problem (Mycelium's reading): The vulnerability of riparian and coastal areas, waterfront cities, and islands to climate change impacts such as storm surges, flooding, erosion, sea level rise, and extreme events, and the need for innovative solutions to increase their resilience and ecological functions.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Testing and demonstrating innovative solutions and Nature-based Solutions (NbS) through at least 6 demonstration activities in real conditions, utilizing an integrated source-to-sea approach, transboundary actions, and living labs to achieve TRL 6-8.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Riparian and coastal areas, waterfront cities, and islands within the Atlantic and Arctic, Mediterranean, Baltic and North Sea, or Danube River basins (including deltas and the Black Sea).
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

This topic aims at directly engaging with and supporting riparian and coastal areas, waterfront cities and islands and their communities in demonstrating and accelerating the transitions needed for achieving one or several objectives of the Mission “Restore our Ocean and Waters”. The participation of relevant public bodies managing those areas and their communities as partners of the consortium is strongly encouraged.

Project results are expected to contribute to all the following outcomes:

- Member States and Associated Countries are provided with cost-effective and innovative solutions to increasing riparian and coastal areas’ resilience to climate change, especially in waterfront cities and islands, contributing to reach the targets of the EU climate adaptation and water resilience strategies for 2030, but also supporting achievements of the EU biodiversity strategy for 2030, the Water Framework and the Marine Strategy Framework directives;

- Enhanced ecological functions of riparian and coastal areas including in waterfront cities and islands (e.g.: water quality improvement, pollution remediation, erosion control, morpho-dynamics and sediment transport, biodiversity conservation and restoration);

- Reduced vulnerability to climate change related risks (e.g.: lowering flood risks by increasing their natural buffer capacity; adapting to sea level rises and extreme events, and enhancing drought resilience by increasing groundwater recharge functions, carbon sequestration, reducing harmful algal blooms, etc.) with biodiversity co-benefits;

- Increased socio-economic benefits deriving from protecting and restoring riparian and coastal areas and from the remediation of pollution, as well as for recreational and touristic activities;

- Stakeholders and local competent authorities managing riparian and coastal areas, including in waterfront cities and islands (not limited only to those who are partners in the consortium), are engaged to implement and upscale innovative solutions that contribute to increasing resilience to climate change and water-related risks, including by strengthening synergies with their own programmes and resources and encouraging public and private investment.

Scope:

Riparian and coastal areas play a critical role in local climate regulation and serve as the buffer regions between land and waterways, providing a wide array of important ecosystem services such as acting as natural barriers against storm surges, flooding, and erosion, filtering pollutants from the water, regulating floods, providing habitats for species and increasing soil health. sequestering carbon. Islands, which offer invaluable natural resources that support people, cultures and livelihoods, are particularly vulnerable to climate change.[1]

Proposals are also encouraged to consider -- where relevant -- the services offered by European research infrastructures[4]. #25 [grant] Circularity of seafood supply chain
Amount: €1,000,000–€8,925,000
Link: https://ec.europa.eu/info/funding-tenders/opportunities/portal/screen/opportunities/topic-details/HORIZON-MISS-2027-03-OCEAN-02
Still open/current: yes
Deadline (application): 2027-09-21
Abstract:
Expected Outcome:

Project results are expected to contribute to all of the following expected outcomes:

- Measurable improvements in the competitiveness and increased environmental sustainability of the EU’s fisheries and/or aquaculture sectors by integrating circular economy principles;

- Minimized and better managed waste products derived from fisheries and/or aquaculture sectors as well as improved reutilization and reduction of by-products;

- Reduced existing barriers preventing the implementation and development of circular principles in seafood chains, such as the cost of advanced processing technologies, regulatory hurdles, lack of collaboration across the different seafood supply chain actors or limited market demand and acceptance;

- Measurable socio-economic benefits for local stakeholders and communities involved in the seafood processing chain.

Scope:

Proposals under this topic are expected to show how activities and results will contribute to achieve Mission objective 2 - prevent and eliminate pollution of marine and freshwaters and Mission objective 3 – Sustainable, carbon-neutral and circular blue economy.

The goal is to improve the competitiveness of the European seafood industry along the value chain while ensuring optimal resource use and minimising environmental impacts by applying circular economy principles to the aquaculture and/or fisheries sectors.

In this topic, seafood covers marine or freshwater edible organisms, including seaweeds and algae.

Projects under this topic are relevant to the Circular Economy Action Plan, the EU Bioeconomy Strategy, the EU Algae Initiative, the EU Action Plan Towards Zero Pollution, the European Ocean Pact and the Mission objective of making the blue economy sustainable.

The circular approach in seafood supply chain can be applied by the reduction and better management of waste products and/or by improving the valorisation of fisheries and aquaculture by-products which can be used as input for other industries. The aquaculture sector can also explore more sustainable and circular practices as following the example of the Integral Multi-tropic Aquaculture (IMTA) or the diversification to lower trophic species. Another example is the use of innovative organic feed from fisheries bycatch, agriculture products or low-trophic species, as alternatives to traditional fish meal and fish oil, which will reduce dependency on wild fish stocks.

Proposals under this topic should test and demonstrate the technical feasibility, the economic viability and the effectiveness of innovative solutions that improve the circularity and the sustainability of the seafood chain of aquaculture and/or fisheries sectors. These circular solutions should also provide socio-economic benefits to the local communities and stakeholders across the seafood value chain by creating jobs and business opportunities, and enhance skills at local level.

Proposals should address at least one of the following issues:

- Innovative and efficient methods and techniques for extracting high-value compounds and valorising seafood by-products from discards of unavoidable unwanted catches or waste products (e.g.: fish sludge, fish manure, trimmings, viscera, shells, seaweed and algal residues, etc.). These high-value extracted compounds can be used for different applications, such as animal feed, or as inputs for other industries like, for instance, food production, fertilisers, nutraceuticals, cosmetics, biotech industries, bioplastics and bio-based packaging. Applications in the field of alternative energy sources or pharmaceuticals are excluded under this topic.

- Innovative organic feed ingredients, as alternatives to fish meal and fish oil, with the potential to support good growth and Feed Conversion Ratio (FCR) taking into account single species nutritional needs, enabling sustainable future organic aquaculture development in Europe.

final_text:
Here's what I found across both projects.

## The two most urgent deadlines

**1. Sandia National Laboratory – John von Neumann Postdoctoral Fellowship in Computational Science** — application due **2026-11-18 (in 2 days)**, from the lab's feed (#12). It's a one-year (renewable) postdoc in computational science and data-driven methods, with a strong emphasis on machine learning, numerical analysis, and uncertainty quantification.

**2. International Conference on Web Search and Data Mining (WSDM)** — manuscript due **2026-11-18 (in 2 days)**, also from the lab's feed (#13).

Both are due the same day, so they're effectively tied for most urgent.

## Who in the lab fits each

For the **Sandia fellowship**, the nightly ranking's profile fit puts **Tomás Ferreira-Lind** (#6) closest (63% match, declared interests in circulation/turbulence and physics-informed ML), with **you** (#2, 62%, data assimilation with ML) and **Priya Raman** (#4, 58%, satellite oceanography) behind. Tomás's physics-informed ML background is the strongest single fit for a computational-science postdoc; your data-assimilation profile is a close second.

For the **WSDM manuscript**, the ranking names **Sun-hee Park** (#5, 59%, ocean data tools) as closest, then **Jonah Whitcombe** (#3, 58%, marine litter / Lagrangian analysis) and **Priya Raman** (#4, 57%). Sun-hee's data-tools focus is the natural lead author for a data-mining systems paper.

One caveat: Mycelium hasn't read the requirement slots for either call yet, so these are profile-fit matches only, not a confirmed slot-by-slot coverage. If you want, I can dig into the specific requirements and map each member's declared/demonstrated evidence against them.

## Which recent paper would strengthen each

**For the Sandia fellowship (computational science / ML):**
- **#38 Ocean-E2E: Hybrid Physics-Based and Data-Driven Global Forecasting of Marine Heatwaves with End-to-End Neural Assimilation** (2026) — a hybrid physics + data-driven MHW forecasting framework with end-to-end neural assimilation, 40-day forecasts, outperforming state-of-the-art ocean numerical/AI models. This is the strongest single paper to show a candidate working at the intersection of ML, data assimilation, and operational ocean forecasting — exactly the fellowship's domain.
- **#47 The interface of data assimilation and machine learning** (2026, Bach) — a survey of the ML–DA interface. Useful as a framing reference to position the applicant's work within the emerging field, especially for your data-assimilation profile.

**For the WSDM manuscript (data mining / web & data):**
- **#34 Multi-horizon forecasting of coastal high water temperature events for operational marine-heatwave early warning in South Korean aquaculture** (2026, Kang et al.) — a walk-forward benchmark of eleven statistical and deep-learning models on a five-year hourly in-situ panel from 30 coastal stations, with calibrated probabilistic prediction intervals. This is a strong, concrete data-mining/ML benchmarking paper that fits the WSDM style and directly supports the Marine heatwave early warning project.
- **#33 Plastic polymer classification with shortwave infrared reflectance** (2026, Ohall et al.) — develops and benchmarks polymer-type classification algorithms (SSPI, MSPC) for marine debris remote sensing. If the WSDM submission is anchored in the Plastic pathways project, this is the better fit, since it's squarely about ML classification and data analysis of debris.

So the pairing depends on which project the WSDM paper serves: **#34** if it's heatwave/forecasting, **#33** if it's debris/plastic. For the Sandia fellowship, **#38** is the clear lead.

Want me to pull the full requirement slots for either call and do a proper member-by-member coverage check?

#38 [paper] Ocean-E2E: Hybrid Physics-Based and Data-Driven Global Forecasting of Marine Heatwaves with End-to-End Neural Assimilation
Authors: Ruiqi Shu, Ruijian Gou, Yanfei Xiang, Xiaomeng Huang
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.1145/3770855.3818893
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
This work focuses on the end-to-end forecast of global extreme marine heatwaves (MHWs), which are unusually warm sea surface temperature events with profound impacts on marine ecosystems. Accurate prediction of extreme MHWs has significant scientific and financial worth. However, existing methods still have certain limitations in forecasting general patterns and extreme events. In this study, to address these issues, based on the physical nature of MHWs, we created a novel hybrid data-driven and numerical MHWs forecast framework Ocean-E2E, which is capable of 40-day accurate MHW forecasting with end-to-end data assimilation. Our framework significantly improves the forecast ability of MHWs by explicitly modeling the effect of oceanic mesoscale advection and air-sea interaction based on a dynamic kernel. Furthermore, Ocean-E2E is capable of end-to-end MHWs forecast and regional high-resolution prediction, allowing our framework to operate completely independently of numerical models while outperforming the current state-of-the-art ocean numerical/AI forecasting-assimilation models. Experimental results show that the proposed framework performs excellently on global-to-regional scales and short-to-long-term forecasts, especially in those most extreme MHWs. Overall, our model provides a framework for forecasting and understanding MHWs and other climate extremes. The source code is available at https://github.com/ChiyodaMomo01/Ocean-E2E.

#33 [paper] Plastic polymer classification with shortwave infrared reflectance: Opportunities and limitations for remote sensing of marine debris.
Authors: Ohall, Ashley, Koestner, Daniel, Bisson, Kelsey, Brandes, Jay, Garaba, Shungudzemwoyo P, Rivero-Calle, Sara
Venue: Marine pollution bulletin
Year: 2026
Link: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42600411/
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Marine plastic debris or litter poses urgent environmental, socio-economic, and human health challenges, yet tools for polymer-specific detection with optical remote sensing remain limited. To advance optical classification capabilities, the newly curated and comprehensive MArine Debris spectral reference Library (MADLib) collection was used to evaluate three existing algorithms and develop two proof-of-concept approaches for polymer type classification with hyperspectral shortwave infrared (SWIR) reflectance measurements. A stepwise classification framework was designed to identify seven polymer types from hyperspectral reflectance data, known as the six-step polymer identification (SSPI) algorithm. SSPI achieved an overall classification accuracy of 89%, which declined to 73 ± 1% when simulated Gaussian noise was added to the measurements. Although performance declined under simulated noisy conditions, the framework establishes a foundation for future refinement through other avenues, such as spectral matching or machine learning methods. A multispectral polymer type classifier (MSPC) approach was also developed and evaluated using machine learning methods to leverage diagnostic features in SWIR reflectance data from only eight moderately-broad bands. A shallow neural network showcased strong performance for a subset of the seven most represented polymers in MADLib under the relatively restrictive testing procedures explored, achieving consistent and noise-robust class accuracies over 80%. The MSPC approach highlights the promise of compact multispectral systems for efficient and scalable polymer type identification. Overall, this work highlights both the potential and current limitations of reflectance-based polymer type identification and guides the next generation of remote sensing approaches for marine plastic debris.

results.content:
#34 [paper] Multi-horizon forecasting of coastal high water temperature events for operational marine-heatwave early warning in South Korean aquaculture: a walk-forward benchmark of eleven statistical and deep-le
Authors: Young-Jin Kang, Ki-Hwan Kim, Seok Chan Jeong
Venue: Frontiers in Marine Science
Year: 2026
Link: https://doi.org/10.3389/fmars.2026.1887350
Still open/current: yes
Abstract:
Introduction High water temperature (HWT) marine-heatwave events along the southern coast of South Korea cause repeated mass mortalities in cage aquaculture of olive flounder (Paralichthys olivaceus), rock bream (Oplegnathus fasciatus), red sea bream (Pagrus major) and Korean rockfish (Sebastes schlegelii). Existing operational forecasts rely on coarse numerical ocean models that lack the temporal granularity and site specificity required by farm managers, while the recent wave of deep-learning sea surface temperature (SST) models has been tuned almost exclusively on smoother open-ocean grids. Methods We present the Hybrid GNN-BiLSTM, a 3.1 M-parameter graph–temporal architecture combining a weighted spatial GNN with a BiLSTM temporal core, reversible instance normalization (RevIN) and a persistence skip connection, and benchmark it against ten alternatives – three reference baselines (Persistence, Seasonal-naïve, Climatology), the ARIMAX statistical model, four lightweight or linear deep models (DLinear, PatchTST, N-HiTS, CNN-LSTM) and two attention-based models (Informer, Temporal Fusion Transformer) – on a five-year hourly insitu panel from 30 monitoring stations along the Tongyeong–Geoje–Yeosu coast (2020–2025) under a unified rolling-origin walk-forward protocol (720 h lookback, 168 h horizon, one forecast per station every 24 h across a 12-month validation window). Marine-heatwave detection is scored at tiered 26/28/30 °C operational thresholds. Results The Hybrid GNN-BiLSTM achieves the lowest 1 h RMSE (0.057 °C), 0.85 °C at h = 72 and 1.24 °C at h = 168, with the highest long-horizon residual skill of any deep model on this panel (SS_res = 0.71 at h = 72). CNNLSTM attains the lowest mean horizon root-mean-square error (RMSE = 0.636 °C) thanks to a nearly flat error curve, and PatchTST is competitive at short-to-medium horizons (0.694 °C mean). The Hybrid GNN-BiLSTM reaches F1 = 0.82 at 26 °C and F1 = 0.65 at 28 °C, and a probabilistic Gaussian negative-log-likelihood head supplies calibrated 90 % prediction intervals without post-hoc recalibration. Discussion A 38 h mean advisory lead time was demonstrated in the 2024 NIFS regional HWT alert period, indicating that a site-specific graph–temporal model can deliver operationally actionable early warning for coastal aquaculture.

Authors: Eviatar Bach

Still open/current: yes
Problem (Mycelium's reading): The interface of machine learning (ML) and data assimilation (DA), specifically how ML can be integrated with the process of combining model forecasts with observations to optimally estimate the state of chaotic systems such as the atmosphere.
Method (Mycelium's reading): Overview/survey of main topics and methods at the interface of ML and DA.
Setting (Mycelium's reading): Operational forecasting centres worldwide, with particular emphasis on chaotic systems such as the atmosphere.
Abstract:
Data assimilation (DA) is the process of combining forecasts from a model with observations in order to optimally estimate the state of a system. This is critical for chaotic systems, such as the atmosphere, since if observations are not continually assimilated the model will quickly lose skill. DA is routinely performed (usually every 6 hours) at operational forecasting centres around the world. In this article we discuss the interface of machine learning (ML) and DA. This is still an emerging and quickly developing field, and this article tries to give an overview of some of the main topics and methods.
